questions.text: In 'Forgot password', what does 'look up user' do when the email is not registered? Does the flow stop, and what does the browser see?
questions.about: Forgot password: submit email -> look up user

questions.text: What does 'rate limit: 3 per hour' count: per email, per IP, or something else? What does the user get when the limit is hit?
What exactly is in the emailed link, and what does the server store in reset_tokens? How does 'validate token' match the link to a row?
Does 'respond' wait for the email to be sent, or only for the job to be put on the Email queue?
What is the Email queue (what technology, where does it live), and what does the API server put on it?
What does 'the usual retries' mean for the Email worker: how many, how spaced, and what happens to the job after the last failure? Does the user ever find out?
questions.about: The email worker has the usual retries

questions.text: When is the token marked as used: when the link is opened, or when the password is saved? What if the new password fails the policy check: can the user retry with the same link?
questions.about: Links last 30 minutes and work once

questions.text: What does the user see if the token is expired, already used, or invalid, at 'Open link' and at 'Set password'?
questions.about: Open link: validate token -> show new-password form

questions.text: In 'save password' through 'revoke sessions', are these steps in one database transaction? What if the process fails between saving and revoking?
questions.about: Set password: save password -> revoke sessions

questions.text: How is the new password stored (hashing), and what does 'breached-list check' call: a local list or an external service? What happens if that check is unavailable?

answers.text: If no user has that email, the flow stops. The browser gets the same generic message as for a known address and nothing is sent. Required so addresses cannot be probed.

It counts per account (reset_tokens rows created for that user in the last rolling hour), not per IP. At 3 or more, the user still gets the generic message but no token is created and no email is sent. Per account is what the brief requires.
The link contains the raw 32-byte token only. reset_tokens stores user id, SHA-256 hash, issued time, expiry and used flag. Validation hashes the token from the URL and looks up the row by hash.
Respond waits only for the job to be put on the Email queue, not for the send. This keeps the response the same for known and unknown addresses and does not depend on the mail provider.

The existing email queue's technology and location are not known to me; the brief says only that the API adds a job and the worker sends it. The design needs nothing more than that. The job holds the recipient and the link.

From the brief: the worker retries up to 3 times with backoff, then logs the failure and drops the job. The user is never told; they can request a new link, subject to the hourly limit. Spacing of backoff is not specified and not needed by this design.
The link is marked used when the password is saved, in the same transaction. A policy failure leaves it live, so the user can retry until expiry. Opening the link does not use it.
In both Open link and Set password, an invalid, expired or used token shows the same page: 'this link has expired, request a new one'. Brief requires the check at both points.

Yes, saving the password, marking the link used and deleting the user's sessions are one transaction, so a failure between them rolls everything back and the link stays live. The confirmation email is queued after commit.

The brief does not say which hash algorithm login uses, so I only say to reuse the existing one. It also does not say whether the breached list is local or an external service. I decided that if the check is unavailable the password is rejected with 'try again later' and the link stays live, which is the simplest safe handling. Both facts are listed under Open questions.

questions.text: What does 'kill the account's live links' do to the old rows: delete them, mark them used, or set them expired? Do killed rows still count toward the 3-per-hour limit?
questions.about: Forgot password: one transaction: kill the account's live links, insert new row

questions.text: How does the token get from the new-password form shown in step 2 to the Set password request in step 3? Does the form carry it, or does the page keep it somewhere?
What is the condition on that update, and what does the user see when their submit loses? Is the transaction rolled back, including the password change?
questions.about: Marking it used is a conditional update inside the transaction, so a second submit loses

questions.text: What is a session here and what happens to a user who is logged in on other devices when the password is set? Does that include the browser doing the reset?
questions.about: delete all of the user's sessions

questions.text: Who is this email sent to, what does it say, and what happens if queuing it fails after the transaction has committed?
questions.about: put "password changed" email job on the queue

questions.text: What happens if putting the job on the Email queue fails? Is the new token row already committed, and what does the browser see?
questions.about: Forgot password: put "send reset email" job on the Email queue (contains the link)

answers.text: Killing a link means setting its used flag, not deleting the row. Rows must stay so the hourly limit can count them, so yes, killed rows still count toward the 3 per hour. This is the simplest option and needs no extra column.
The token is in the URL of step 2. The form page puts it in a hidden field, and the submit sends it back with the new password. Nothing else keeps it. Added to the diagram.

The condition is: update the row where id matches, used is false and expiry is later than now. If it changes 0 rows, another submit already won or the link just expired. The transaction is rolled back, so the password is not changed, and the user sees the 'expired' page. Added to the diagram.

From the brief: a session is one row in sessions per logged-in device. Deleting all of the user's rows logs out every device, including the browser that did the reset, which is then redirected to login. Added to Terms.

It goes to the account's email address and says the password was changed. If queuing fails after commit, the password stays changed (the commit cannot be undone), the failure is logged and there is no retry. This is the simplest handling and the user still reaches the login page. Added to the diagram and notes.

Yes, the token row is already committed. The failure is logged and the browser still gets the generic message, so the response is the same for every case and leaks nothing. The user never gets that link; they can request again, and the attempt counts toward the hourly limit. I chose not to add a retry or compensating delete, to keep it simple. Added to the diagram and notes.

teachbacks.text:
1. Request password reset (flow 1). The user cannot log in and submits their email on the forgot-password form. The browser sends the email to the API server.
2. User lookup. The API looks the email up in the users table in Postgres. If no user is found, it stops. Nothing is sent, and the browser gets the generic message "If an account exists for that address, we've sent a link." This is the same message the user gets in every other case, so the response doesn't reveal whether an account exists.
3. Rate check. The API counts reset_tokens rows for this account created in the last hour. These rows are never deleted and they include links that a newer request killed. If the count is 3 or more, it stops with the generic message and sends nothing. The limit is per account, not per IP.
4. Issue the link. The API generates a reset token (32 random bytes). In one Postgres transaction it marks all of this account's live links as used, then inserts a new reset_tokens row. The row holds the user id, the SHA-256 hash of the token, the issued time, the expiry (issued + 30 minutes) and a used flag set to false. The raw token is never stored. It exists only in the emailed link.
5. Queue the email. The API puts a "send reset email" job, which contains the link, on the Email queue. If the queue fails, the API logs it. The row stays, and the user still sees the generic message. The API doesn't wait for the send. It responds at once with the generic message.
6. Delivery. The Email queue passes the job to the Email worker, and the worker sends it through the mail provider. The worker retries 3 times with backoff, then logs and drops the job. If the email is never delivered (queue failure or the worker giving up), nobody is told. The user can request a new link, within the hourly limit.
7. Open the link (flow 2). The user clicks the link, and the browser sends the token from the URL to the API. The API hashes the token and looks for a matching row. If the row is missing, expired or used, the user sees the "this link has expired, request a new one" page. If the link is live (unused and not expired), the API shows the new-password form. The form keeps the token in a hidden field.
8. Submit the new password (flow 3). The browser posts the hidden-field token and the new password to the API. The API hashes the token and finds the row again, because the link may have expired or been used since step 7. If the link is not live, the user sees the same "expired" page.
9. Password validation. If the password is under 12 characters or is on the breached list, the API shows an error, and the link stays live so the user can retry until it expires. If the breached-password check is unavailable, the API rejects the password with "try again later" and keeps the link live.
10. Commit the change. The API opens one transaction. First it marks the link used with an update where id = the row and used = false and expiry > now. If 0 rows are updated, a second submit won, so the transaction rolls back and the user sees the "expired" page. This conditional update is what makes a double submit safe. If the update succeeds, the transaction saves the new password hash. The hash is made the same way as login passwords today. It also deletes all of the user's session rows in the sessions table, which logs out every device, including the one doing the reset. If any part fails, nothing changes, the user sees an error, and the link stays live.
11. Notify. The API puts a "password changed" email job on the queue. The email goes to the account's address and says the password was changed. If the queue fails, the API logs it. The password stays changed, and there is no retry.
12. Finish. The API redirects the browser to the login page. There is no automatic login. The user logs in with the new password, and that creates a new session.

Note on step 12: the last sentence (a login creates a new session) is my inference. The document only says there is no automatic login and that sessions are rows in a table.
gaps: The document doesn't say which hash algorithm login passwords use. It only says the reset must reuse it, so I can't say how the new password is hashed in step 10.
The document doesn't say whether the breached-password list is a local file or an external service. So I can't explain what the check does in step 9 or how it can fail.

The document doesn't say what makes a row a particular account's "live link" beyond the user id, or how the link in the email is built from the token. For example, it doesn't say whether the token travels in the path or the query string, or which URL and page the link points to.
The document doesn't say how the browser reaches the forgot-password form or how the token gets into the URL parameters the API reads. It describes only the API-side logic, not the UI routes.
